b: Both kingdoms run down. The north falls to Assyria in 722 BC; the south survives longer under a few good kings but falls to Babylon, with Jerusalem and the temple destroyed around 586 BC.
The book ends with a small note of hope: the exiled king of Judah is released from prison and eats at the Babylonian king's table. The line is not extinguished.

5.t: A Syrian general healed after being insulted by the simplicity of the instruction. Jesus cites this at Nazareth.

17.t: The writer stops the narrative to explain the theology of the exile in one long paragraph.

25.t: The temple burned, the walls broken, the people taken. The book ends with a released king eating at a foreign table — a very small door left open.

2.t: Elisha asks for a double portion, the inheritance of a firstborn son rather than twice the power.

6.t: The servant sees only the army. Elisha prays and he sees the hills full of horses and chariots of fire. Then the captured raiders are fed and sent home.

18.t: He removed the high places and broke up the bronze serpent, which the people had been burning incense to. Even a genuine relic can become an idol.

19.h: Spreading the letter before the LORD
19.t: Hezekiah takes the threat into the temple and lays it out. A model of what to do with a letter you cannot answer.

22.h: The book found in the temple
22.t: Josiah tears his clothes when it is read, because nobody had known what it said. Reform follows from rediscovery.

4.t: It keeps flowing while there are jars to fill. The limit is set by what she gathered.
She builds a room for the prophet and later loses the son she was given. Her refusal to be comforted takes her straight to Elisha.

7.t: They find the enemy camp abandoned and say to each other: this is a day of good news and we are keeping it to ourselves.

13.t: The king strikes three times and Elisha is angry that he stopped. A strange episode about half-hearted obedience.

20.t: Hezekiah is told to put his house in order, weeps, and is given an extension. Read chapter 20 to the end before deciding it was a blessing.

23.t: The most thorough reform in Israel's history, and the writer still says God's anger was not turned away. Reform from the top does not change hearts.

24.t: The first deportations, including the young men Daniel is among.

1.h: Is there no God in Israel
1.t: Ahaziah sends to consult Baal-Zebub. Elijah's question exposes it.

3.t: Water comes without wind or rain. The preparation is commanded before the provision appears.

8.t: She arrives at the exact moment the king is hearing her story. Providence in timing.

9.t: Her death fulfils Elijah's word precisely.

10.t: He destroys Baal worship but keeps the golden calves. Zeal that stops exactly where it would cost him.

11.t: A queen kills the royal family, and one baby is hidden in the temple for six years. The line of David survives by a single child.

12.t: A chest with a hole in the lid, and workers so honest no accounts were needed.

14.t: He spares the sons of his father's assassins, obeying the law of Moses. Then pride leads him into an unnecessary war.

15.t: Several reigns in a few verses, with assassinations and short tenures. Israel's end is coming fast.

16.t: He copies a pagan altar from Damascus and installs it in the temple.

21.t: The worst king in Judah's history, fifty-five years long. Chronicles records his repentance; Kings records the damage. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

18.ctx: About 715 BC. Hezekiah, son of the faithless Ahaz, becomes king of Judah. The northern kingdom of Israel has already fallen to Assyria (722 BC, recalled in verses 9–12), and Judah is an Assyrian vassal paying tribute.
18.mean: Hezekiah is given one of the highest ratings of any king in Kings: he ‘did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, just as his father David had done’, and ‘no king of Judah was like him, either before him or after him’. He removed the high places, the local shrines where worship had drifted into Canaanite practice. He smashed the sacred pillars and Asherah poles. He even broke up Nehushtan, the bronze snake Moses made (Numbers 21:4–9), because people were burning incense to it. A genuine relic of God’s past saving work had become an idol. Hezekiah ‘trusted in the LORD’, held fast to him, and kept his commands, and the LORD was with him. So he rebelled against the king of Assyria and defeated the Philistines. Then the writer pauses to recall the fall of Samaria. Israel was exiled ‘because they did not listen to the voice of the LORD their God’. The two kingdoms stand side by side: one destroyed for unfaithfulness, one led by a king who trusts.
18.big: Hezekiah is the model of a king who trusts the LORD, even to the point of destroying a sacred object that had become an idol.
18.diff: The dates in this chapter are hard to fit together. Verse 1 places Hezekiah’s accession in Hoshea’s third year (before 722 BC), but verse 13 puts Sennacherib’s invasion of 701 BC in Hezekiah’s fourteenth year, which implies an accession around 715 BC. Many scholars explain this through a period of co-regency with Ahaz, or different ways of counting reigns. Others think one of the figures has been miscopied. The overall setting is not in doubt.

b: In 2015 Eilat Mazar’s Hebrew University excavation on the Ophel, at the foot of the Temple Mount, found a small clay seal impression (a bulla) reading ‘Belonging to Hezekiah [son of] Ahaz king of Judah’. It was found in a refuse dump from Hezekiah’s time or shortly after.

The seal shows a two-winged sun flanked by Egyptian-style ankh symbols. Royal symbols of this kind were common across the region; the excavators suggest the design dates from late in Hezekiah’s reign.

18.ctx: 701 BC. Hezekiah has joined a revolt against Assyria with Egyptian backing (compare Isaiah 30:1–5). The new Assyrian king, Sennacherib, sweeps down the coast to crush it.
18.mean: ‘Sennacherib king of Assyria attacked and captured all the fortified cities of Judah.’ After the glowing introduction, this comes as a shock. The king who trusted the LORD loses almost his whole kingdom. Hezekiah sends to Sennacherib at Lachish: ‘I have done wrong; withdraw from me, and I will pay whatever you demand.’ The price is 300 talents of silver and 30 talents of gold, about ten tonnes of silver and one of gold. To pay it, Hezekiah empties the temple and palace treasuries and strips the gold from the temple doors he had himself overlaid. The writer does not comment, but the contrast with verses 5–7 is deliberate. Hezekiah’s first move under pressure is the old political one of buying off the enemy, and it does not work.
18.big: Faithfulness does not exempt God’s people from crisis, and buying peace from the world does not bring it.

b: Sennacherib’s campaign is one of the best documented events in the Old Testament. His annals survive on clay prisms (the Taylor Prism in the British Museum, and others in Chicago and Jerusalem). In them he says he took 46 of Hezekiah’s walled cities and countless villages, deported 200,150 people, and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem ‘like a caged bird’.

Where the records agree. Both sides record Judah’s fortified cities falling (18:13), Hezekiah sending tribute (18:14–16) and Jerusalem surrounded (18:17). Both give the gold as 30 talents. The silver differs: 300 talents in the Bible, 800 in the Assyrian record. Exaggeration in royal propaganda, a different way of counting, or extra payments sent later have all been suggested.

What the annals leave out. The annals never claim that Jerusalem fell. Hezekiah was the leader of the revolt, yet he stayed on his throne, and the tribute was sent on to Nineveh afterwards. Other rebels on this campaign were not so fortunate. Sennacherib replaced Luli, king of Sidon, who fled and died in exile, and he executed the nobles of Ekron. An Assyrian king who had taken the rebel leader’s capital would have said so. The silence fits the Bible’s account that the siege of Jerusalem ended without the city being taken.

src.l: D. J. Wiseman, ‘Sennacherib’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)
John W. Olley, The Message of Kings, The Bible Speaks Today (IVP, 2011)

hist.t: Lachish: the siege in stone and in the ground
b: Lachish, one of Judah’s most important fortified cities, about 40 km south-west of Jerusalem, was Sennacherib’s headquarters (18:14, 17; 19:8). In his palace at Nineveh he had the siege carved in a continuous series of reliefs lining a central room. They show slingers and archers attacking, battering rams pushed up ramps, defenders throwing torches, captives led away, rebels impaled, and Sennacherib on his throne receiving the plunder. The reliefs are now in the British Museum, displayed in a room of about the same size as the original.

The ground confirms the stone. Excavations (Starkey 1932–38, Aharoni 1966–68, Ussishkin 1973–87) found the Assyrian siege ramp at the south-west corner, a counter-ramp the defenders built inside the walls, hundreds of arrowheads, sling stones and pieces of armour, and mass burials of about 1,500 people in nearby caves.

A point of honesty: Lachish was a major victory, not a minor one. It was a great fortress, and the reliefs show the siege accurately. But it is striking that the king chose Lachish, not Jerusalem, as the centrepiece of his palace. As Tyndale House puts it, Sennacherib ‘was not able to take the crown jewel’. The reliefs celebrate the victory he did win.

b: The king’s jars. Large numbers of storage-jar handles stamped lmlk, ‘belonging to the king’, together with one of four place names, have been found across Judah. The excavations at Lachish showed that these jars belonged to a royal supply system set up before Sennacherib’s invasion, which most archaeologists attribute to Hezekiah (compare 2 Chronicles 32:27–29).

Hezekiah’s tunnel. 2 Kings 20:20 and 2 Chronicles 32:30 say Hezekiah brought the water of the Gihon spring into the city. A tunnel over 500 metres long, cut through solid rock, still carries it under the City of David. An inscription found inside it in 1880 (now in Istanbul) describes the two teams of diggers cutting towards each other until they met ‘axe to axe’. Some scholars once dated the tunnel centuries later. In 2003, though, radiocarbon dating of plant material in the plaster and uranium–thorium dating of cave deposits, published in Nature, placed it around 700 BC. That is Hezekiah’s time, as the Bible says.

18.ctx: Despite the tribute, Sennacherib sends three senior officials with a large army from Lachish to Jerusalem. Their titles, Tartan (commander-in-chief), Rabsaris (chief official) and Rabshakeh (chief cupbearer, here the spokesman), are known from Assyrian records.
18.mean: The Rabshakeh stands at the very spot where Isaiah had once challenged Hezekiah’s father to trust God (Isaiah 7:3), and makes a masterful propaganda speech. He attacks every source of hope in turn. Egypt is ‘that splintered reed of a staff that will pierce the hand of anyone who leans on it’. The LORD? Hezekiah has removed his high places and altars, so surely God is offended. That is a clever misreading of Hezekiah’s reform. Besides, he claims, ‘The LORD himself said to me, “Go up against this land and destroy it.”’ When the officials ask him to speak Aramaic, the diplomatic language, rather than Hebrew in the people’s hearing, he deliberately turns to the people on the wall. Do not let Hezekiah deceive you. Make peace and you will each eat from your own vine until I take you to a land like your own. Then comes the climax: ‘Has the god of any nation ever delivered his land from the hand of the king of Assyria?’ Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Samaria: their gods failed. The people stay silent, as Hezekiah commanded, and the officials bring the speech to the king with their clothes torn.
18.big: The enemy’s strongest weapon is the argument that God cannot or will not save; the question of the chapter is whether the LORD is just another national god.

src.l: John W. Olley, The Message of Kings, The Bible Speaks Today (IVP, 2011)
D. J. Wiseman, ‘Sennacherib’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)

19.ctx: Hezekiah’s response to the Rabshakeh’s speech. Isaiah the prophet, whose ministry spans the reigns of Uzziah to Hezekiah (Isaiah 1:1), enters the story.
19.mean: This time Hezekiah’s first move is the right one. He tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth, and goes into the house of the LORD. He sends his officials to Isaiah with a picture of helplessness: ‘Children have come to the point of birth, but there is no strength to deliver them.’ His hope rests on one thing: the Assyrian has mocked ‘the living God’. Perhaps the LORD will hear and rebuke him. Isaiah’s answer is brief and calm: ‘Do not be afraid of the words you have heard… I will put a spirit in him so that he will hear a rumor and return to his own land, where I will cause him to fall by the sword.’ The whole rest of the story is the fulfilment of these two sentences.
19.big: When God’s name is mocked, his people can bring the matter to him and leave the defence of his honour in his hands.

src.l: John W. Olley, The Message of Kings, The Bible Speaks Today (IVP, 2011)

19.ctx: Sennacherib has moved on from Lachish to Libnah, nearby. News comes that an Egyptian and Nubian army is advancing.
19.mean: The Rabshakeh returns to find his king fighting at Libnah, and Sennacherib hears that Tirhakah king of Cush is marching against him. This is the first stage of Isaiah’s ‘rumour’. Rather than withdraw, Sennacherib sends a letter to Hezekiah that sharpens the earlier speech. Do not let ‘your God in whom you trust’ deceive you. Look at the list of kingdoms and their gods that Assyria has destroyed. The challenge is now aimed directly at the LORD’s trustworthiness.
19.big: The conflict is no longer between two kings but between the king of Assyria and the God of Israel.

b: The problem. Tirhakah (Egyptian Taharqa) of Egypt’s Nubian 25th Dynasty reigned c. 690–664 BC. But the campaign of 2 Kings 18–19 happened in 701 BC, when he was not yet king.

Where the majority of scholars stand. The New Bible Dictionary notes that most scholars regard the mention of Tirhakah as an anachronism. Many therefore suggest the biblical account merges Sennacherib’s campaign of 701 BC with a second, later campaign against Jerusalem during Tirhakah’s reign. That would also explain why Sennacherib’s murder (19:37) seems to follow soon after.

The case for the biblical account as it stands. Egyptologist K. A. Kitchen argues that Tirhakah, a royal prince, could well have commanded the Egyptian and Nubian force in 701 BC. He was called ‘king’ because that is what he was by the time the account was written down, much as we might say ‘Queen Elizabeth was born in 1926’. An argument once used against this, that Tirhakah was too young in 701, has been answered by specialists. On the other side, the two-campaign theory has a serious weakness: neither the surviving Assyrian annals nor the Babylonian chronicles mention any second campaign against Judah. And the Bible does not say how long after his return Sennacherib died. ‘He returned to Nineveh and stayed there’ covers twenty years. A single campaign in 701 BC, as the text presents it, remains a reasonable reading of the evidence.

19.ctx: Hezekiah takes the letter into the temple. This prayer is one of the great prayers of the Old Testament, repeated in Isaiah 37.
19.mean: Hezekiah spreads the letter out before the LORD and prays. He begins with who God is: ‘O LORD, God of Israel, enthroned between the cherubim, you alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made the heavens and the earth.’ Then he faces the facts honestly. It is true that the Assyrian kings have destroyed these nations and thrown their gods into the fire, ‘for they were not gods, but only wood and stone—the work of human hands’. Sennacherib’s list proves less than he thinks: of course idols could not save. Last comes the request, and its purpose: ‘Save us from his hand, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone, O LORD, are God.’ Hezekiah’s chief concern is God’s glory among the nations, not just his own survival.
19.big: Faithful prayer starts with who God is, tells him the truth about the situation, and asks for help so that his name will be known.

src.l: John W. Olley, The Message of Kings, The Bible Speaks Today (IVP, 2011)

19.ctx: Isaiah’s reply to Hezekiah’s prayer: a poem addressed to Sennacherib, then a sign for Hezekiah, then a direct promise.
19.mean: ‘I have heard your prayer concerning Sennacherib king of Assyria.’ The poem turns the tables. ‘The Virgin Daughter of Zion’, apparently defenceless, despises and mocks the invader and shakes her head as he leaves. Sennacherib boasted of his own achievements, crossing mountains and drying up rivers. But God says he planned it all ‘long ago’. Assyria was only ever the tool of God’s purposes (compare Isaiah 10:5–19). Because of his arrogance God will put ‘my hook in your nose and my bit in your mouth’, the way a captive or a beast is led (compare Amos 4:2), and lead him back the way he came. Then comes a sign for Hezekiah. For two years the people will eat what grows by itself, because the fields have been ravaged, and in the third year they will sow and reap again. A remnant will take root. Finally the promise: the king of Assyria ‘will not enter this city or shoot an arrow into it… or build up a siege ramp against it’. ‘I will defend this city and save it for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David.’
19.big: The proud empire that thinks it controls history is only an instrument in God’s hand, and he will defend his people for his own name’s sake.
19.diff: Some find a tension between ‘he will not… build up a siege ramp against it’ (19:32) and Sennacherib’s claim to have hemmed Jerusalem in with earthworks. The prophecy concerns a full assault on the city, which never happened. The Assyrian claim describes a blockade, which both sides agree happened (18:17).

src.l: John W. Olley, The Message of Kings, The Bible Speaks Today (IVP, 2011)
D. J. Wiseman, ‘Sennacherib’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)

19.ctx: The fulfilment, told in three short verses.
19.mean: ‘That very night the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 men in the camp of the Assyrians.’ The writer gives no details, only the result: in the morning the camp was full of dead bodies. Sennacherib broke camp, returned to Nineveh and stayed there. Every part of Isaiah’s word is fulfilled. Not an arrow was shot at the city. The king went home by the way he came. And one day, worshipping in the temple of his god Nisroch, he was killed by his own sons, who escaped to Ararat, while Esarhaddon reigned in his place. The writer passes over the twenty years between his return and his death (see the drop-down), because the point is not the timing but the outcome. The king who asked which god could save from his hand was not saved by his own.
19.big: God delivers his people by his own power, and those who mock him come to nothing.

hist.t: What happened to the Assyrian army?
b: What is agreed. Sennacherib’s campaign ended without the capture of Jerusalem, and he went home with Hezekiah still on the throne. His own annals agree with the Bible on this (see the note on 18:13).

The Bible’s account. ‘That very night the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 men in the camp of the Assyrians.’ The Bible gives the cause as God’s direct action and does not describe the means.

Herodotus. Writing in the fifth century BC, the Greek historian Herodotus records a story he heard from Egyptian priests (2.141). When ‘Sanacharib, king of the Arabians and Assyrians’ marched against Egypt, its priest-king Sethos prayed in his god’s temple. That night, near Pelusium on Egypt’s border, field mice swarmed the Assyrian camp and ‘gnawed quivers and bows and the handles of shields’, so the army fled and many were killed. It is a different location and a different explanation. But it is an independent, non-Israelite memory of a sudden disaster striking Sennacherib’s army through divine action after prayer.

Plague? Herodotus does not mention disease. The link many scholars have suggested is an inference, but a reasonable one. In the ancient world, swarms of rodents went together with epidemics. The Bible itself pairs rats with a plague of tumours (1 Samuel 6:4–5). And elsewhere in Scripture ‘the angel of the LORD’ is the agent of plague: in 2 Samuel 24:15–16 and 1 Chronicles 21:12, a plague sent on Israel is carried out by ‘the angel of the LORD ravaging every part of Israel’. The Jewish historian Josephus (first century AD) describes the disaster as ‘a pestilential distemper’ sent by God, and presents this as the account of the Babylonian historian Berossus. How much of that passage really comes from Berossus is uncertain.

The critical view. Many scholars treat the Herodotus story as Egyptian legend with little historical value. Many also regard the figure of 185,000 as impossibly large, or as a later exaggeration. Some suggest that numbers using the Hebrew elef (‘thousand’) could originally mean military units. Those who read the account as a later composition also see the swift death of Sennacherib in 19:37 as compressing twenty years.

The strongest case for the biblical account. Three independent kinds of evidence point the same way. Assyrian records are silent where a victory would be expected. Hezekiah was left on his throne. And a separate Egyptian tradition remembers Sennacherib’s army suffering a sudden, divinely sent catastrophe. A plague in a crowded military camp is entirely plausible, and Scripture elsewhere uses this very language for one. The Bible does not need Herodotus to be right in detail. The point is that the outside evidence is consistent with Jerusalem’s deliverance being sudden and decisive, exactly as the Bible says.

b: Sennacherib was assassinated in 681 BC, twenty years after the campaign. The Babylonian Chronicle records that he was killed by his son in a rebellion. His younger son Esarhaddon, already named crown prince, describes in his own inscription the turmoil with his brothers that followed, and he succeeded to the throne, just as verse 37 says. The Bible names the assassins as Adrammelech and Sharezer; versions of these names also appear in later Greek writers quoted by Josephus and others.
The irony the writer intends is plain. Sennacherib mocked the God of Israel as unable to save. He died at the hands of his own sons in the temple of a god who could not save him.
